_cross_item: Strong cross-item pattern in the B items: 'k is any real constant, so every admissible integer value of x, y or the intercept gives exactly one k'. B2, B4, B6, B9 and B10 all rest on it, and in each count item the integer-k reading is offered as a distractor (B2:6, B4:8, B6:19). A student who learns this from one item answers the others; in the count items the key is never the integer-k count. A second shared distractor recipe is summing the counted variable instead of k (B1:496, B9:153), and both are struck by sign. A third is the endpoint off-by-one sibling placed next to the key (B2:11/12, B5:184/3 vs 187/3, B6:42/43), which creates a lone-adjacent-pair tell pointing at the key region. A2 and A7 are one template (anchor point, two-endpoint interval bound, count of integer values at an extrapolated x), and A4 is a close variant. B1/B7, B2/B9 and B4/B10 are near-template pairs. STAGE 2 EXTENSION: the keyed file confirms the pattern is systematic. EVERY B item (B1-B10) carries an 'integer values of k only' distractor (B1:-27, B2:6, B3:7, B4:8, B5:21, B6:19, B7:20, B8:13, B9:-22, B10:19/2), and every explanation names 'k need not be an integer' as the key step. Across the batch, 'never pick the integer-k answer' is a reliable cross-item tell, and all ten B items share one meta-template: real parameter, integer condition on a derived quantity, then count, sum, extreme or mean over k. Recommend at most 1-2 B items per form, and that A2/A7 never share a form.
